newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-PEOPLE'S SUNDAY DECIMATES WOMEN'S SEEDS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PEOPLE'S SUNDAY DECIMATES WOMEN'S SEEDS.

text.p: Wimbledon's middle Sunday proved an unhappy experience for six women's seeds, including former champion Conchita Martinez, who all slipped up on the lush grass at the All England Club.

As well as the 10th-seeded Martinez, the extra day saw the end of Lindsay Davenport (5), Amanda Coetzer (6), Anke Huber (7), Brenda Schultz-McCarthy (14) and Barbara Paulus (16) to leave only three seeds in the top half of the draw occupied by Martina Hingis.
Martinez, who beat Martina Navratilova to take the title in 1994, could not raise her game to match that of lofty Helena Sukova, the 1.88 m tall veteran of 16 successive Wimbledon championships.
Sukova, 31, who has reached the quarter-finals five times here, serve-and-volleyed the Spaniard, whose game was honed on Iberian clay, out of the third-round match 6-4 6-2.

Martinez, seeded 10, looked out of sorts playing on Sunday's traditional rest day, after a rain-plagued week forced organisers to re-jig the schedule and open the gates to an appreciative public at reduced prices.

While queues for prized seats were still winding three km round the ground, Davenport and South Africa's Coetzer, playing second-round matches, were quickly dispatched from courts four and 18 at opposite ends of the All England Club.

Davenport, the Olympic champion and a quarter-finalist here three years ago, went down 7-5 6-2 to a representative of the up and coming generation of Czech players in Denisa Chladkova, 12 years younger than Sukova and ranked 57 in the world.
Davenport blamed the weather. "This week was so weird. I played on Monday and then to wait till Sunday was a real throw-off," she said.
The American conceded the problem of interrupted play and two full days lost to rain, was the same for everyone, but added: "This is the definitely the weirdest Grand Slam I've played."

Coetzer, 25, the French Open semifinalist, said she took the waiting in her stride but had not had enough practice on grass, when she came up against Patricia Hy Boulais, the 31-year-old Canadian who has been on the circuit almost as long as Sukova.
"I got rushed off the start and then I ended up missing my shots," Coetzer said.
The pair slugged it out from the baseline most of the match. But when Hy Boulais attacked she won points at the net -- 24 winners to Coetzer's four.
It took her just over an hour to earn a third-round berth 6-2 6-1.
A little later Belgium's Sabine Appelmans put paid to Schultz-McCarthy's hopes, downing the Dutch 14th seed on court three 6-2 6-3 in their third round match.
Appelmans, 25, is ranked only four places below Schultz-McCarthy at 19 and reached the fourth round here last year.
Austria's Paulus was the fifth seed to bite the turf, losing 5-7 6-3 6-3 to Naoko Kijimuta of Japan.

But it was not all bad news for the top women. Second seed Monica Seles, third seed Jana Novotna fourth seed Iva Majoli and ninth seed Mary Pierce all got plenty of grass practice winning testing three set matches.
Seles came through against American Kristina Brandi 5-7 6-3 6-3 in a match held over in fading light from Saturday.

The stately Pierce, obviously having some trouble with her elbow which she massaged between games, beat Virginia Ruano Pascual of Spain 6-0 2-6 6-3 and Novotna played her customary peak and trough game to beat Elena Likhovsteva of Russia 6-1 4-6 6-4.
Majoli, the French Open champion, needed physiotherapy on her back and saved a match point against 322nd-ranked Briton Karen Cross, before winning through 4-6 7-6 6-4.
Huber was the day's final victim, beaten 3-6 6-4 6-4 in the gathering gloom by 16-year-old Russian Anna Kournikova who is proving a sensation on her Wimbledon debut.

If she can beat Sukova in the last 16, she will attract even more attention than Hingis, who danced through to the fourth round by defeating American Nicole Arendt 6-1 6-3, looking unworried, unhurried and full of confidence.
